content: The EMX1 homeobox protein is a protein in humans encoded by the EMX1 gene. The EMX1 gene belongs to the EMX family of transcription factors. This gene, along with other members of its family, is expressed in the developing cerebrum, also known as the telencephalon. EMX1 is involved in defining positional identity, promoting the proliferation of neural stem cells, guiding the differentiation of neurons into specific layer-dependent phenotypes, and determining whether cells will adopt a neuronal or glial fate. The exact function of the EMX1 transcription factor remains unclear. However, its widespread presence during corticogenesis suggests that it may play a role in establishing the cellular identity of cortical neurons. Mice with the EMX1 gene knocked out (Emx1 -/-) are viable and exhibit only mild defects, which are confined to the forebrain. Histological and molecular analyses reveal that the structure of the cerebral cortex in these mice appears normal. However, the hippocampus is typically smaller, and the most significant defect is the complete absence of the corpus callosum. The majority of EMX1 transcripts are detected in the nuclei of cells within the developing telencephalon, including the prospective cerebral cortex, olfactory bulbs, and hippocampus. EMX1 is present in nearly all cortical neurons during their proliferation, migration, differentiation, and maturation, although its levels vary. Around birth and shortly thereafter, EMX1 levels increase in cortical layers V and VI as well as in the subplate (SP). Both EMX1 and EMX2 play critical roles in regulating the development of the dorsal telencephalon and are among the earliest genes expressed in pallial-specific regions. During embryonic development, the telencephalon gives rise to a diverse array of neuronal and glial cells, which migrate to their final positions in the mature cerebral cortex and basal ganglia. The embryonic telencephalon is divided into the dorsal pallium and ventral subpallium, which later develop into the mammalian cerebral cortex and basal ganglia, respectively. The dorsal telencephalon is further subdivided into distinct pallial domains, each of which contributes to specific neuroanatomical regions of the mature brain. The ventral telencephalon is also divided into two progenitor domains. These dorsal and ventral telencephalic domains can be distinguished during embryogenesis by their unique gene expression patterns, which are regionally restricted and contribute to the specification of telencephalic areas. In the developing mouse embryo, EMX genes are primarily expressed in extensive regions of the rostral brain, including the cerebral cortex, olfactory bulbs, and olfactory epithelium. EMX1 gene expression is restricted to the dorsal telencephalon. Until postnatal stages, EMX1 expression is associated with cortical neurogenesis, differentiation, migration, and the formation of synaptic connections. This indicates that EMX1 plays a crucial role in defining the identity of the developing cortex. EMX1 is not limited to the telencephalon; it is also expressed in branchial patterns and the apical ectodermal ridge of developing limbs. Within the dorsal telencephalon, EMX1 expression is observed slightly anterior to the boundary between the diencephalon and telencephalon. EMX1 is expressed in most cortical neurons within the developing telencephalon, regardless of whether the neurons are proliferating, migrating, or differentiating. This widespread distribution of EMX1 transcripts in the developed cerebral cortex suggests its importance in cortical development. However, the intensity of EMX1 transcript expression varies significantly depending on the developmental stage. Around birth and shortly thereafter, EMX1 transcripts are absent from the marginal zone (MZ) but become more prominent in cortical layers V and VI as well as in subplate neurons. In these regions, EMX1 may contribute to the development of early functional circuitry and the specification of distinct cellular identities. The distribution of EMX1 is so pervasive in the developing brain that it is found in the cerebral cortex, olfactory bulbs, dentate gyrus, and hippocampus in midand late-gestation embryos as well as in postnatal mice. The zinc finger transcription factor GLI3 has been identified as a regulator of EMX1. In GLI3 Extra-toes mutants, where the GLI3 transcription factor is mutated, the expression of both EMX1 and EMX2 genes is lost.
